Because every present key maps to itself, a hit returns `raw`, and a miss returns the default `raw or "obj"` — which is also `raw` whenever `raw` is truthy — the whole expression is exactly `raw or "obj"` for every possible input, including the empty string produced by the `except` path a few lines above. Replacing the lookup with `return raw or "obj";` and deleting the table is behaviour-preserving for all inputs, not just the enumerated ones.

`_prefetch_types` (lines 3353-3379) defines five nested wrappers — `get_types_class`, `get_typing_class`, `get_builtin_class`, `get_enum_class`, `get_jac_builtin_class` — that are byte-identical except for which module field they pass: each is `return as_class_type(self._get_type_from_module(self.<X>_module, type_name));`. That is five three-line functions to bind one already-available argument. A single `get_class(module, type_name)` replaces all five, turning e.g. `get_builtin_class("int")` into `get_class(self.builtins_module, "int")` at each of the roughly thirty call sites in the same function body, which stay one line each. Behaviour is preserved because the wrappers add nothing beyond the module argument — `as_class_type` is itself a nested helper at 3354-3359 that returns the value when it is a `types.ClassType` and `None` otherwise, and it is applied identically in all five.

`collect_foreign_structs` inlines at lines 36-42 the exact type-name resolution that the module already exposes as `declared_type_name` (lines 54-66) and that `collect_foreign_fns` uses at lines 95-97: check for `uni.Name` and take `.value`, otherwise take `.value` if it is a `str`, otherwise nothing. Replacing the inlined block with `tname = declared_type_name(var.type_tag.tag) if (var.type_tag and var.type_tag.tag) else None;` mirrors what the sibling collector already does for parameters. One caveat I confirmed by reading both: the inlined version guards with `tag?.value and isinstance(tag.value, str)`, so an empty-string `.value` yields `None`, whereas `declared_type_name` returns `""`; the difference is only observable for a struct field whose declared type name is the empty string, which no parser output produces. The two collectors also share an identical ten-line scaffold (skip `None` modules, `get_all_sub_nodes(typ=uni.Import)`, skip imports without `clib_decls`, iterate `imp.clib_decls`) that a single generator over clib declarations would cover once.

summary: `query` (lines 28-63) and `query_range` (lines 81-123) are the same 36-line function written twice. I read both bodies line by line: both resolve the base URL and bail on falsy, both wrap the same `import requests` / `from requests.exceptions import RequestException` in a try/except ImportError that calls `_warn_once` with the identical key `"requests-missing"`, both check `resp.status_code != 200`, both check `body.get("status") != "success"`, both return `_extract_result(body)`, and both have the same two trailing except arms (`RequestException` -> "Prometheus unreachable", bare `Exception` -> error). The only differences are the URL suffix (`/api/v1/query` vs `/api/v1/query_range`), the params dict, the default timeout (3.0 vs 5.0), and the word "query" vs "query_range" inside four log strings. The simpler shape is one private `_promql_get(path, params, timeout, label)` holding the body, with `query` and `query_range` reduced to building their params dict and calling it; passing the operation name as `label` reproduces all four log strings character-for-character, and because both branches already share the `_warn_once` key the import-warning behaviour is unchanged (only the first call of either ever logs).

`ProcessGateway` is a 37-line wrapper that only forwards to `MicroserviceGateway`. All five of its fields (registry, port, host, client_dist_dir, static_mounts) are passed straight through to the `MicroserviceGateway` constructor with no transformation; `setup()` builds one and calls its `setup()`; `serve()` lazily calls `self.setup()` then `self._gateway.start()`. I grepped the whole repo for `ProcessGateway` and found exactly two construction sites, both in jac/jaclang/scale/runtime/orchestrator/orchestrator.jac (lines 78 and 109), and both immediately call `.serve()` and nothing else — neither touches `.setup()`, `._gateway`, nor the `middleware` field it inherits from `Gateway`. There are zero test references (the tests under tests/microservices and tests/server construct `MicroserviceGateway` and `EmbeddedGateway` directly). Inlining is behaviour-preserving: replace each call site with `MicroserviceGateway(...)` built from the same kwargs, then `.setup()` and `.start()`, which is the exact sequence `serve()` performs. Note the knock-on that the `Gateway` base in runtime/gateway/gateway.jac would then have a single implementation (`EmbeddedGateway`), though `EmbeddedGateway` does genuinely use the inherited `middleware` registry at embedded_gateway.impl.jac:135, so the base itself still earns its keep.

`service_call` (lines 9-116) and `walker_call` (lines 119-203) repeat several spans verbatim. I diffed them by hand: the httpx import guard (48-55 vs 144-151) is character-identical including the error string; the outbound header assembly (57-72 vs 153-167) is identical apart from blank lines — same Authorization from `get_current_auth()`, same X-Trace-Id from `get_current_trace()`, same lazy `current_traceparent` import and traceparent header; the retry scaffolding (74-78 vs 169-173: max_attempts=3, backoff=0.1, last_err, `_sv_rpc_timeout(module_name)`) is identical; and the retry-and-backoff except arm (101-108 vs 188-195) is identical. The simple, low-risk extraction is two private helpers — `_build_rpc_headers() -> dict[str, str]` for the 15-line header block and `_require_httpx()` for the 8-line import guard — called from both functions. That is behaviour-preserving because neither block reads any local state beyond the contextvars it already imports, and it leaves the genuinely divergent parts (SSE detection and `_unwrap_sv_envelope` in service_call, the plain post and `_hydrate_walker_envelope` in walker_call) untouched. I deliberately scope this to the two identical helpers and not the whole retry loop, whose bodies really do differ.

`get_mongo_client` (41-53), `get_redis_client` (55-67) and `get_firestore_client` (69-81) are the same 12-line memoising getter written three times: call `require_optional(pkg, capability)`, call `_resolve_uri(arg, DatabaseType.X)`, insert into a module-level dict if absent via `DatabaseProviderFactory.create_client(DatabaseType.X, uri=resolved)`, return the cached entry. I read all three in full — the only differences are the two `require_optional` string arguments, the enum member, which of `_mongo_clients`/`_redis_clients`/`_firestore_clients` is used, and the local variable name in the firestore copy. The simpler shape is one private `_cached_client(cache, package, capability, db_type, key)` helper with the three public functions reduced to one-line delegations (keeping their existing signatures, including firestore's `project_id` parameter name so no caller changes), plus a single close loop iterating over the three dicts.

`core_api` (52-62), `apps_api` (65-75) and `networking_api` (78-88) are three copies of the same 11-line function. I read all three verbatim: each guards on `if not _ensure_config() { return None; }`, then wraps a single kubernetes client constructor in try/except Exception, logging `f"<ApiName> init failed: {e}"` at warning level and returning None. The only variation is the constructor called (`client.CoreV1Api` / `client.AppsV1Api` / `client.NetworkingV1Api`) and the matching name inside the log string — which happens to be exactly the attribute name, so a single `_api(name: str)` helper doing `getattr(client, name)()` and logging `f"{name} init failed: {e}"` reproduces all three log lines character-for-character. `UtilityFactory.create_logger` is a factory with exactly one product. Of its three branches, only 'standard' constructs anything; 'cloudwatch' and 'elasticsearch' raise NotImplementedError and anything else raises ValueError. I grepped the repo for `create_logger` and found four production call sites — plugin.jac:221, plugin.jac:274, sdk/client.jac:155 and runtime/realizer/kubernetes_realizer.jac:55 — every one of which passes the literal `'standard'` and no config. Since `StandardLogger.init` (standard_logger.jac:5) discards its config argument entirely, `create_logger('standard')` is exactly `StandardLogger()`. The factory is also not the construction seam for the `Logger` interface: the second implementation, `EventLogger` (sdk/events.jac:5), is instantiated directly at sdk/client.jac:152, bypassing it. The simpler shape is to drop `create_logger` and construct `StandardLogger()` at the four call sites. Flagging honestly: tests/deploy/test_factories.jac (lines 91, 101, 145, 181) and tests/test_deploy_k8s.jac call `create_logger` including its default-argument path, so those would need updating alongside — hence the raised risk.

Inside `parse_storage_quantity` (lines 244-290) the suffix-matching loop is written twice — once over `suffixes_binary` (265-275) and once over `suffixes_decimal` (276-286) — and the two loop bodies are byte-for-byte identical: endswith check, strip the numeric part, raise the same `f"Storage quantity '{quantity}' is missing a numeric component."` on empty, return `int(number_part) * multiplier`. The simpler shape is one loop over a single dict built as binary-then-decimal. I checked that merging preserves match order exactly: the binary keys (Ki, Mi, Gi, Ti, Pi, Ei) all end in a lowercase 'i' while the decimal keys (k, M, G, T, P, E) end in their own letter, `str.endswith` is case-sensitive, and so no input string can match both a binary and a decimal suffix — the binary-first precedence that the current two-loop ordering encodes is therefore never actually exercised as a tie-break, and a single ordered dict reproduces it regardless. I checked the neighbouring `parse_memory_quantity` (29-61) as a merge candidate too and deliberately excluded it: it upper-cases its input and returns float, so 'K' means 10^3 there while `parse_storage_quantity` requires lowercase 'k' and returns int — folding them together would change what callers observe.

`DeployFactories` (lines 12-15) plus `_load_deploy_factories` (17-21) is a carrier object holding two `type` fields whose only purpose is to defer two imports. Four separate functions hand-roll the identical 'mtime-keyed jac.toml cache' pattern: `_load_pins` (placement_pins.jac:10-43), `npm_dependency_names` (placement_pins.jac:112-158), `client_framework` (placement_pins.jac:163-196), and `_load_cut` in the sibling `service_cut.jac:8-36`. (Note: `sealed.py:_read_section` is a deliberate pure-Python bootstrap twin documented at sealed.py:101-103 and pinned by a twin test — it is NOT part of this collapse.)

`_get_cache_dir` (cli_boot.jac:14-25) re-implements, branch for branch, the platform resolution that `jac0core/cache_paths.py` exists to own. cache_paths.py's own module docstring says the platform-resolution logic 'lives in exactly one place'; its `get_jir_cache_dir()` (lines 26-36) has the identical three arms — `LOCALAPPDATA` (defaulting to `~/AppData/Local`) then `jac/cache/...` on win32, `~/Library/Caches/jac/...` on darwin, `$XDG_CACHE_HOME` or `~/.cache` then `jac/...` elsewhere — differing only in the final path component (`jir` vs `bytecode`). `NATIVE_ABI_VERSION` is declared twice in the same package with the same value and no link between them. `codeinfo.jac:332` declares `glob NATIVE_ABI_VERSION: int = 1` and stamps it into every emitted layout via `NativeModuleLayout.abi_version` (codeinfo.jac:335); `native_dylib.jac:4` re-declares its own `glob NATIVE_ABI_VERSION: int = 1` and validates incoming sealed layouts against that private copy in `layout_from_dict` (lines 73-79), raising when they disagree. summary: `jac/jaclang/runtimelib/impl/client_runtime_core.impl.jac` (788 lines, the browser client runtime) and `jac/jaclang/runtimelib/client/impl/client_runtime_core.impl.jac` (436 lines, the platform-hook client runtime used by the react-native target) are two copies of the same client runtime core.
